arena.dominant_form: Single-piece or 2-pack rectangular/L-shaped memory-foam pad with a fabric cover and a non-slip rubber base, sized to run along the desk edge under one forearm
arena.summary: Page one is a small, brand-fragmented field of four confirmed sellers (VAYDEER, Jelbows, Leolee, FUZADEL) rather than one runaway winner, with the memory-foam desk-edge pad as the shape roughly half the tiles converge on (F1, F2, F4, F9). It is a fight over foam thickness/density credibility and price anchoring around $13-17, not a brand moat war — VAYDEER leads on review count and shape validation but has not locked out the term (F1, F9).

brand_dominance.evidence: VAYDEER's flagship L-shaped foam pad holds 2,045 reviews at 4.6 stars, roughly 2x the next-largest confirmed competitor (Jelbows, 1,100+ reviews) and 3-4x VAYDEER's own smaller variants (543-605 reviews), showing real pull toward this brand and shape but no listing clears the 3,500-review dominance threshold (F1, F2, F3).
brand_dominance.deep_study: VAYDEER wins on size/thickness perception (its own listing title leads with 'Upgraded Larger and Thicker') and on a 4.6-star rating backed by a real review base, which buyers read as proof the shape works. It is weak exactly where the category's biggest complaint cluster lives: C1 (35% of negative sentiment, stage 4) says pads still let the hard desk edge press through, meaning even the review leader has not convincingly solved density/thickness for heavier or bonier forearms, and none of VAYDEER's own product images or copy visibly address desk-lip fit or foam depth (per scout's unanswered questions). We coexist by not attacking VAYDEER on price or review count directly, and instead flank on a named, testable foam-density/thickness spec plus a diagram-based fit image (raised lip, glass desks, left/right use) that closes the exact gaps its own buyers and the unanswered-questions list surface.

months_to_first_clone.assumption: A foam-pad-in-fabric-cover shape needs no registered tooling beyond a standard foam die-cut and sewn cover, both commodity capabilities at Chinese contract factories already supplying VAYDEER/Leolee-style pads; a private-label reseller can source a near-identical mold and list within 4-8 weeks of seeing a page-one entrant gain traction.

clone_price_usd.assumption: Clone price floor anchors to the observed page-one low ($8 for basic small pads, F9) with a base case slightly under the $13-17 cluster median, since a quantity-first seller undercuts on price rather than compete on foam quality or finishing.

copycat_risk.why: The visible differentiator (a thicker/larger foam pad shape) is a thumbnail-visible geometry with no patented mechanism, no hard-to-source named component, and no clamp/hardware complexity like FUZADEL's tray; any factory already producing foam desk pads can retool a similar profile quickly, making this an easy, fast-follow clone category unless a specific spec or registered design is called out.

price_war.why: At launch, alone with a differentiator that directly answers the category's #1 complaint (C1: pad feels too thin/firm, 35% of negative sentiment) against a field where the leader hasn't visibly solved it, the product can plausibly be a top pick on the page. Once quantity-first clones fill the grid at $8-13 with similar-looking foam shapes, buyers scanning thumbnails at that price point increasingly can't tell the density difference without reading reviews, pushing the listing down to roughly third choice behind VAYDEER's banked review count and the cheapest clone, taking a meaningful bite out of forecast volume.

moats.moat: Registered design on the desk-edge profile geometry (the specific L-shaped/dual-taper cross-section and thickness callout)
moats.why: A quantity-first cloner sourcing from a generic foam-pad factory will not risk a design-registration dispute over a shape they can approximate slightly differently for near-zero extra cost; it doesn't stop all copying but it stops exact-mold clones and gives a legal lever exact copies don't have elsewhere in this category.

moats.moat: Named, tested high-density memory foam spec (e.g., a stated minimum foam density/thickness passing a load test) directly answering complaint cluster C1
moats.why: Cheap factories default to the lowest-density foam that holds shape in photos; naming and testing a specific density spec costs only cents-to-dimes more per unit but requires the cloner to source and verify a different foam grade, which a volume-first reseller chasing the $8-13 floor has no incentive to do since it erodes their price advantage.

moats.moat: Dimensioned fit diagram + packaging insert addressing raised-lip/glass-desk/left-right use (the three gaps in scout's unanswered_questions)
moats.why: A printed insert and diagram-based main/secondary images cost a few dimes per unit in packaging and photography but require design effort a poly-bag reseller skips entirely; it's a weak moat on its own since it's copyable, but it raises the bar just enough that the fastest, cheapest clones won't bother replicating it in their first wave.

competitor_profiles.name: VAYDEER Upgraded Larger and Thicker Elbow Rest Pad, Desk Wrist Rest
competitor_profiles.strength: Largest review base and highest rating (4.6) on page one, with a 'larger and thicker' positioning that visually signals more cushioning in a thumbnail; the single L-shaped pad is the category's dominant winning shape by a 3-4x review-count margin over the brand's own smaller variants.
competitor_profiles.weakness: Despite the size/thickness claim, no visible evidence (diagram, spec callout) that it solves the category's top complaint (C1: still feels the desk edge through the pad); no answer to raised-lip, glass-desk, or left/right-use questions in its listing.

competitor_profiles.name: Jelbows Ergonomic Gel Wrist Rest Set for Arms & Elbows (2 Pack)
competitor_profiles.strength: Second-largest confirmed review base; 2-pack format gives buyers a left/right or spare-pad value story at a similar price point to a single foam pad.
competitor_profiles.weakness: Gel surface reported to turn sticky and develop a plastic smell over weeks of use (C2, 30% of negative sentiment) — a durability failure that a foam-and-fabric construction avoids entirely.

competitor_profiles.name: Leolee Elbow Rest Pads for Desk, Memory Foam & Non-Slip Base (2 Pack)
competitor_profiles.strength: Cheapest credible foam-pad option in a 2-pack format with a non-slip base, praised for comfort and elbow-pain relief — closest direct shape/price competitor to our planned variant.
competitor_profiles.weakness: Buyers report they can still feel the hard desk surface through the pad (C1), the same insufficient-density failure as the category leader, suggesting the whole foam-pad field underinvests in this spec.

competitor_profiles.name: FUZADEL Ergonomic Rotating Desk Elbow/Arm Support Tray
competitor_profiles.strength: Differentiated mechanism (aluminum clamp-on rotating tray) rather than a simple cushion, appealing to buyers who want adjustable positioning, not just padding.
competitor_profiles.weakness: Thin/hard cushion pad on top of the tray and an unstable-feeling clamp connector (C3, 20% of negative sentiment) undermine trust in the core mechanism; higher price with a hardware failure mode a simple pad doesn't have.

watch_signals: New page-one sellers adopting the same 'larger and thicker' L-shaped foam-pad silhouette or copying a named foam-density spec once we publish one.
Any page-one listing (especially Leolee or a new entrant) dropping price below the current $13-14 floor, signaling a quantity-first clone wave has started.
Review velocity of VAYDEER and any new entrants versus our own listing's pace, to see if the review-count gap is closing faster than expected.
Whether a competitor starts explicitly marketing a fit-diagram or 'works on raised lip/glass desks' claim, showing the flank we're using is being closed.
